part_a.q_equation: Q_{t+1}(s_t, a_t) = (1 - \alpha) Q_t(s_t, a_t) + \alpha(r_t + \gamma \max_{a'} Q_t(s_{t+1}, a'))

alpha.name: Learning Rate
alpha.description: Controls how much new information overrides old information. Range: [0, 1]
alpha.role: Determines the step size of Q-value updates. Higher α means faster learning but potentially less stable. Lower α means slower but more stable convergence.
alpha.typical_values: Common values: 0.1 to 0.5. Often decayed over time (e.g., α_t = α_0 / (1 + t))

gamma.name: Discount Factor
gamma.description: Determines the importance of future rewards. Range: [0, 1]
gamma.role: Higher γ (close to 1) makes the agent value long-term rewards more. Lower γ (close to 0) makes the agent focus on immediate rewards. Essential for handling infinite-horizon problems.
gamma.typical_values: Common values: 0.9 to 0.99. γ=0 means only immediate reward matters, γ=1 means future rewards are equally important.

epsilon.name: Epsilon (ε-greedy policy)
epsilon.description: Probability of selecting a random action instead of the greedy action. Range: [0, 1]
epsilon.role: Balances exploration vs exploitation. ε=1 means pure exploration (random), ε=0 means pure exploitation (greedy). Often decayed over time to shift from exploration to exploitation.
epsilon.typical_values: Common values: Start with 0.9-1.0, decay to 0.01-0.1. Decay schedule: ε_t = max(ε_min, ε_max * decay^t)

off_policy_explanation.definition: Off-policy means the algorithm learns the value of the optimal policy while following a different (behavior) policy.

explanation.behavior_policy: The policy used to select actions (e.g., ε-greedy policy)
explanation.target_policy: The policy being learned (greedy policy: always select action with highest Q-value)
explanation.key_insight: Q-learning updates Q-values using the maximum Q-value of the next state (greedy action), regardless of which action was actually taken. This allows learning the optimal policy while exploring.

contrast_with_on_policy.on_policy_example: SARSA is on-policy - it learns the value of the policy it follows
contrast_with_on_policy.difference: SARSA uses Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) where a_{t+1} is the action actually taken. Q-learning uses max_a Q(s_{t+1}, a) regardless of action taken.

advantages: Can learn optimal policy while exploring
Can use data from any policy (e.g., expert demonstrations)

issue1.description: Learning rate that is too high or too low can cause convergence problems

too_high.symptom: Q-values oscillate or diverge, unstable learning
too_high.cause: Large updates cause overshooting, Q-values bounce around optimal values
too_high.example: α = 1.0 causes complete replacement of old values, no learning stability

too_low.symptom: Extremely slow convergence, requires many episodes
too_low.cause: Tiny updates mean Q-values change very slowly
too_low.example: α = 0.001 requires millions of steps to converge

solutions.description: Start with higher α (e.g., 0.5-1.0) and decay over time (e.g., α_t = α_0 / (1 + decay_rate × t))
solutions.rationale: Allows fast initial learning, then stabilizes as Q-values approach optimal

solutions.description: Use α_t = α_min + (α_max - α_min) × exp(-decay × t)
solutions.rationale: Smooth transition from exploration to exploitation

solutions.solution: State-Action Visit Count Based Learning Rate
solutions.description: Use α(s,a) = 1 / (1 + N(s,a)) where N(s,a) is visit count
solutions.rationale: Decreases learning rate for frequently visited state-action pairs, stabilizing their Q-values

issue2.factor: Insufficient Exploration or Poor Exploration Strategy
issue2.description: Inadequate exploration leads to suboptimal policies and slow convergence

insufficient_exploration.symptom: Agent gets stuck in local optima, converges to suboptimal policy
insufficient_exploration.cause: Early convergence to first reasonable policy found, missing better alternatives
insufficient_exploration.example: ε-greedy with ε=0.01 from start leads to exploitation of poor initial policy

poor_exploration.cause: Pure random exploration doesn't guide learning efficiently
poor_exploration.example: ε=1.0 (pure random) never exploits learned knowledge

solutions.description: Start with high ε (0.9-1.0) and decay to low ε (0.01-0.1): ε_t = max(ε_min, ε_max × decay^t)

solutions.solution: Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) or Optimistic Initialization
solutions.description: Initialize Q-values optimistically high, encouraging exploration of unexplored states
solutions.rationale: Agent naturally explores less-visited states due to optimistic estimates

solutions.description: Use probability distribution: P(a|s) = exp(Q(s,a)/τ) / Σ exp(Q(s,a\')/τ)
solutions.rationale: More systematic exploration based on Q-value estimates, temperature τ controls exploration
